title: Fire and forget
sub: Fire-and-forget, a missing await and async void
cards/0/body:
Calling an async method without await is called fire-and-forget. Inside an async method the compiler warns you about it: CS4014.

A call without await doesn't postpone anything. Remember the state machine (section 3): builder.Start runs the first MoveNext right away. Step by step for the loop below:

  • 1. SaveAsync(o) runs synchronously, on the loop's thread, up to the first await that really waits: the database request has gone out.
  • 2. The method returns an unfinished task. Nobody kept it, so the reference is lost.
  • 3. The loop immediately calls the next SaveAsync without waiting for the first. All the saves run at the same time, even though the code looks sequential.
  • 4. LogAsync writes "saved" while the saves are still running or have already failed.

If the saves share one connection or one DbContext (EF Core), it's also a race. The second call starts an operation before the first one has finished, and EF Core throws InvalidOperationException ("A second operation was started on this context instance…").
cards/1/explain: SaveAsync is called, but nobody waits for its task: the loop moves on, the saves run all at once, and their errors are lost. Write await SaveAsync(o) to save one by one, or collect the tasks and await Task.WhenAll to save them together.
cards/2/q: What ends up in the log?
cards/2/options/0: "saved", even though the saves are still running or have already failed
cards/2/options/1: Nothing: LogAsync won't be called while the saves are running
cards/2/options/2: The log entry appears after all the saves
cards/2/explain: Each SaveAsync call returned at its first pause, and the loop moved on. LogAsync knows nothing about the saves: their tasks were thrown away.
cards/2/wrong/1: A call without await doesn't stop the method: LogAsync runs right after the loop.
cards/2/wrong/2: That would happen with await in the loop or with await Task.WhenAll. Here nobody waits for the SaveAsync tasks.
cards/3/q: SaveAsync saves an order through a shared DbContext (EF Core) and waits for the database. The loop calls it without await for three orders. Where does InvalidOperationException "A second operation was started on this context…" show up?
cards/3/code:
foreach (var o in orders)   // three orders
    SaveAsync(o);           // inside: await _db.SaveChangesAsync()
cards/3/options/0: Inside the later SaveAsync calls: the exception lands in their tasks, which nobody awaits
cards/3/options/1: It's thrown out of the foreach loop on the second call
cards/3/options/2: Nowhere: without await the calls run one after another
cards/3/explain: The first SaveAsync reached the await on the request and returned, but its operation on the context is still running. The next call starts a new operation on the same context, and EF Core throws. The exception is thrown inside an async method, so it lands in the task (section 2) instead of escaping the call. Nobody awaits the task, so nobody sees the error.
cards/3/wrong/1: An async method's exception never escapes the call, even one thrown before the first await: it lands in the task.
cards/3/wrong/2: Without await the loop doesn't wait: the next call starts while the previous one sits at its await.
cards/4/title: What gets lost: the error and the lifetime
cards/4/body:
The error. Each SaveAsync's exception sits in its task (section 2). Nobody awaits the task, so nobody rethrows the exception. UnobservedTaskException fires only when the GC collects the task, and that may never happen.

The lifetime. A task runs until it's done, and it doesn't care whether whoever started it is still alive. The object that created it is no longer needed, the HTTP request has already been answered, and the task is still running. In ASP.NET Core the request's services, such as the DbContext, are destroyed after the response. A task that uses them gets ObjectDisposedException, and nobody sees that either.

The process. In a console app and on a server, continuations run on pool threads, and those are background threads: the process doesn't wait for them. A console program that has returned from Main cuts an unfinished task off mid-sentence.
cards/5/q: What's wrong with fire-and-forget? Select all that apply.
cards/5/options/0: You can't tell when the task finished
cards/5/options/2: The task can outlive the object or request that started it
cards/5/options/3: Calls in a loop run at the same time, even though the code looks sequential
cards/5/options/4: The call itself runs slower than with await
cards/5/explain: Speed has nothing to do with it: a call without await starts the same way as one with await. The problem is control: nobody waits for the task, nobody sees its error, and nobody tracks how long it lives.
cards/6/title: async void: where the exception goes
cards/6/body:
You know the rule from section 2: async void is for event handlers only. Now the mechanism.

An async Task method's builder is AsyncTaskMethodBuilder (section 3): the catch in MoveNext calls SetException, and the exception waits in the task. async void has no task, so the compiler uses a different builder, AsyncVoidMethodBuilder. When it's created, it remembers SynchronizationContext.Current. When MoveNext catches an exception (before the first await or after, it doesn't matter), there's nowhere to put it, so the builder throws it again:

  • there was a context (WPF, WinForms): context.Post(() => throw e). The exception flies out of the UI thread's queue, where none of your try blocks are, and by default the app crashes;
  • there was no context (console, ASP.NET Core, a pool thread): the exception is thrown on a pool thread. An unhandled exception on the pool terminates the process, and on a server that's the whole server with every request.

A try around the call won't help. The call returned at the first pause, and if the exception happened before it, the catch inside MoveNext has already taken it.
cards/6/deep:
In Unity the exception also goes through Post to the UnitySynchronizationContext, but the engine catches it and writes it to the console. The game doesn't crash; the method just silently stops halfway.

AsyncVoidMethodBuilder also tells the context when the method starts and ends (OperationStarted and OperationCompleted). Contexts that wait for every async void are built on this, for example in test frameworks.
cards/7/options/0: After 100 ms the process crashes with an unhandled InvalidOperationException
cards/7/options/2: The exception quietly stays in Fire's task, and the program keeps waiting for input
cards/7/explain: Fire returned at the await, and the try was over. 100 ms later the continuation throws on a pool thread. A console app has no context, so AsyncVoidMethodBuilder throws the exception on a pool thread. An unhandled exception on the pool terminates the process, and ReadLine can't hold it back.
cards/7/wrong/1: By the time of the exception Fire returned long ago, and the try is behind us.
cards/7/wrong/2: async void has no task, so the exception has nowhere to land. It's an unawaited async Task whose exception gets quietly lost.
cards/8/q: Same program, but Fire throws before its first await. Will the catch get it?
cards/8/options/0: No: the catch inside MoveNext took the exception, the builder threw it on a pool thread, and the process crashes
cards/8/options/1: Yes: up to the first await the method runs synchronously on the caller's thread
cards/8/options/2: Yes, but only in a console app, which has no context
cards/8/explain: The first MoveNext does run synchronously, inside the call. But the method body is wrapped in the generated code's try/catch (section 3). That catch hands the exception to the builder, and AsyncVoidMethodBuilder with no context throws it on the pool. Nothing escapes the Fire call.
cards/8/wrong/1: Synchronously, yes, but the exception is caught by the catch inside MoveNext, not by your try.
cards/8/wrong/2: The opposite: a console app has no context, so the exception is thrown on a pool thread and crashes the process.
cards/9/title: If you really must fire and forget
cards/9/body:
Sometimes there really is no need to wait: an email, a metric, a cache warm-up. Then make sure the error isn't lost and that "not waiting" is visible in the code.

  • A wrapper with try/catch inside. RunSafeAsync awaits the work itself and logs the exception. There's nobody outside to catch the error, so it's caught inside the task. The try covers the synchronous part too: work() is called inside it.
  • Discard: _ = task; This is an assignment to a variable that can't be read. It silences CS4014 and tells the reader: not waiting, on purpose. It does nothing else. The task runs the same way, and without a wrapper its exception is lost the same way.
  • On a server, outside the request. Don't carry HttpContext or the request's services into a background task; copy the data beforehand. Long background work goes to a BackgroundService, a .NET host class with an ExecuteAsync(stoppingToken) method. The host starts it at startup and cancels the token at shutdown. Since .NET 6 an unhandled exception in it stops the host by default instead of vanishing. Details in section 6.
cards/10/q: What does _ = change in the line _ = SaveAsync(o);?
cards/10/options/0: It only silences CS4014 and shows you're not waiting on purpose: SaveAsync's error is still lost
cards/10/options/1: It waits for the task synchronously, like .Wait()
cards/10/options/2: It catches the task's exception and logs it
cards/10/explain: A discard is a plain assignment to a variable that can't be read. The task starts and lives exactly as it would without it. To keep the error from getting lost, you need a try/catch inside the task, as in RunSafeAsync.
cards/11/pairs/1/1: Not waiting on purpose, no warning
cards/11/pairs/2/1: Rethrows the exception: to the context or the pool
cards/11/pairs/3/1: The only place a background job's error gets caught
cards/11/pairs/4/1: Host background work outside a request
